_meta.description: Comprehensive micro-step library for TrackIt. Keys: subject → archetype → sub_type → grade_band. Grade bands: high_school (9-10) and advanced (11-12). Steps are plain strings consumed by generateSubtasks() via spaceSteps().

high_school: Set up your workspace — open a blank doc, write the title at the top, phone away
Gather the prompt, rubric, any source texts, and your class notes
Read the prompt twice — underline the key action words and circle the requirements
Brain dump: write everything you know about this topic in bullet points for 5 minutes
Find 2-3 specific pieces of evidence or examples that relate to the prompt
Write 3 different thesis statements — circle the most specific and arguable one
Build a paragraph-by-paragraph outline: intro, body paragraphs, conclusion
BREAK — the planning is done. Take 5 minutes away before writing
Write the introduction — hook, context, thesis last
Write Body Paragraph 1 — topic sentence, evidence, 2-3 sentences of analysis
Write Body Paragraph 2 — topic sentence, evidence, 2-3 sentences of analysis
Write the conclusion — restate argument in new words, why it matters
Read the whole essay aloud — mark anything that sounds off
Check against the rubric — fix anything missing
Format and submit
advanced: Open a working document with two sections: NOTES and ESSAY
Gather all materials — prompt, sources, rubric, class notes
Deconstruct the prompt: identify the task verb, constraints, and write a plain-language restatement
Collect 4-6 pieces of specific evidence with locations — do not start writing yet
Identify the pattern across your evidence — write 3-4 sentences on what it reveals
Draft 3 thesis statements — your thesis must be debatable, specific, and significant
Build a hierarchical outline with counterargument paragraph planned
BREAK — mandatory 5-8 minutes before drafting
Write the introduction — hook strategy, context, thesis
Write Body Paragraph 1 — integrated evidence, 3-4 sentences of analysis
Write Body Paragraph 2 — transition, integrated evidence, analysis
Write Body Paragraph 3 — counterargument, rebuttal, connection to thesis
Write the conclusion — synthesis not summary, resonant closing
Argument coherence check — read only topic sentences in sequence
Read full draft aloud — mark thin analysis and awkward transitions
Rubric audit — confirm thesis, evidence integration, analysis depth
Format and submit

high_school: Set up workspace — open doc, write title and date, phone away
Gather the text, prompt, rubric, and any annotation notes
Read the prompt carefully — what literary element or technique are you analyzing?
Re-read the relevant sections of the text — mark 2-3 key passages
Write what the author is doing with language in those passages — one sentence each
Draft your thesis: [Author] uses [technique] to show [specific argument]
Build your outline — each body paragraph around one piece of evidence
BREAK — 4-5 minutes before writing
Write introduction — context, thesis last
Write each body paragraph — topic sentence, quote with citation, 2-3 analysis sentences
Write conclusion — what does this technique reveal about the text overall?
Read aloud and check that analysis explains WHY not just WHAT
Rubric check and format
Submit
advanced: Set up working document — NOTES section and ESSAY section
Gather text, prompt, secondary sources if required, rubric
Annotate the prompt — identify task verb, scope, and any required analytical lens
Re-read targeted sections — annotate for technique, effect, and textual pattern
Write 4-6 sentences identifying what the author is repeatedly doing and why it matters
Draft 3 thesis statements — push toward: 'By [technique], [author] [claim], suggesting [significance]'
Build full outline — include counterargument or complicating evidence paragraph
BREAK — 6-8 minutes minimum
Write introduction with specific hook strategy — paradox, striking moment, or context
Write Body Paragraph 1 — integrated quote, 3-4 analysis sentences, reconnect to thesis
Write Body Paragraph 2 — transition, integrated evidence, analysis
Write Body Paragraph 3 — complicating or counterargument evidence and response
Write synthesis conclusion — how argument changes how we read the text
Topic sentence coherence check
Full read-aloud — fix thin analysis and unclear transitions
Rubric audit — thesis specificity, analysis depth, evidence integration
Format, citations, submit

high_school: Create research document with three sections: SOURCES, NOTES, DRAFT
Read full prompt — confirm source count, citation format, length requirement
Write one sentence defining your specific topic and angle
Write 3-5 research questions before opening any search engine
Set a 30-minute timer — find all required sources and log them in SOURCES section
Read each source and take notes in NOTES section — only what answers your research questions
BREAK — close all browser tabs before drafting
Build your argument and paragraph sequence from your notes
Write introduction with thesis
Write each body paragraph — evidence with citation, analysis connecting to thesis
Write conclusion — restate thesis, significance, implications
Build Works Cited or References page — every source cited in text must appear here
Read draft aloud — check every fact has a citation
Final rubric check
Format and submit
advanced: Create five-section document: PARAMETERS, QUESTIONS, SOURCES, NOTES, DRAFT
Document all assignment requirements in PARAMETERS section
Write a research question and preliminary hypothesis before searching
Research in priority order: peer-reviewed databases, books, credible journalism — 45-minute timer
Take synthesizing notes — track what sources agree and disagree about, not just what each says
Develop final thesis from evidence — must be argumentative, specific, complex, significant
Build synthesis-based outline — each paragraph around a CLAIM with multiple sources
BREAK — 10 minutes before drafting
Write introduction with contextualized hook and thesis
Write body paragraphs — multi-source synthesis, varied signal phrases, deep analysis
Write counterargument and rebuttal paragraph
Write synthesis conclusion — implications and significance
Build Works Cited — confirm every in-text citation matches and every source is listed
Synthesis audit — no paragraph relies on only one source
Full read-aloud for argument coherence
Final rubric audit
Format and submit

high_school: Open document and write the prompt at the top
Free write for 8 minutes — do not edit, just write everything that comes to mind
Circle the most honest or specific moment in your free write
Write your central claim or insight in one sentence
Build a loose outline: opening scene or moment, development, reflection
Write a full first draft without stopping to edit
BREAK — 5 minutes
Read aloud — mark anything that feels generic or unclear
Revise for specificity — replace abstract statements with concrete details
Check length and format requirements
Final read and submit
advanced: Read the prompt and write a plain-language restatement of what it is asking
Free write for 10 minutes — follow any thread that feels true
Identify the most specific, unexpected, or revealing moment in your free write
Draft 3 possible opening lines — avoid starting with a definition or sweeping statement
Write a central insight in one sentence — what does this essay reveal about you or an idea?
Outline the essay — where does the narrative or argument move? What is the turn?
BREAK — 5 minutes
Write a complete first draft without self-editing
Read aloud — mark any place where the language becomes generic, vague, or performative
Revise for specificity, honesty, and voice
Check that the ending earns its conclusion rather than stating it
Final rubric or prompt check
Format and submit

high_school: Gather all lab records — original data table, observation notes, pre-lab, handout
Read rubric and list every required section — create headings in your document
Write Title and Purpose — specific, includes independent and dependent variable
Copy hypothesis from pre-lab — do not revise it to match results
Write Materials list with quantities and Procedure in numbered past-tense steps
Transfer data table exactly as recorded — do not modify any values
Create graphs — title, labeled axes with units, plotted points, best-fit line if required
BREAK — 5 minutes before analysis
Write Analysis — describe pattern with specific numbers, explain biological mechanism
Write Conclusion — hypothesis evaluation with evidence, 2 error sources with directional effect, 1 improvement
Rubric check — every section present, all graphs labeled, analysis not just summary
Format heading and submit
advanced: Assemble all lab records — notebook pages, observation notes, pre-lab, handout with rubric
Read rubric — list every section with point values, note format requirements
Write Introduction — specific biological mechanism named, research question as final sentence
Write Hypothesis — If/Then/Because with named mechanism and falsification condition
Write Materials with specifications and Procedure at replication-level precision in passive voice
Present data table — correct significant figures, units in all headers, qualitative observations as data
Create graphs — labeled axes with units, error bars if applicable, best-fit line with equation and R²
BREAK — 8 minutes before analysis
Write Analysis — trend with specific numbers, all calculations with full work shown, anomalous data addressed, mechanism explained
Write Conclusion — hypothesis evaluation with quantitative evidence, 3 classified error sources with directional effect, 2 improvements, 1 follow-up question
Scientific accuracy audit — significant figures, units, all claims supported
Full rubric audit
Format and submit

high_school: Gather all lab records — data table, observation notes, pre-lab, handout
List every required section from the rubric — create headings in document
Write Title, Purpose, and Hypothesis from pre-lab materials
Write Materials and Procedure in numbered past-tense steps
Transfer data table — include units in all headers
Create required graphs with labeled axes and units
BREAK — 5 minutes before analysis
Write Analysis — show all stoichiometric or thermodynamic calculations step by step with units
Calculate percent error — show formula, substituted values, and result
Write Conclusion — hypothesis evaluation, 2 error sources, directional effect, 1 improvement
Rubric check — all calculations shown, significant figures consistent
Format and submit
advanced: Assemble all lab records including original notebook pages
Read rubric — note significant figures policy, error analysis requirements, citation format
Write Introduction — chemical principles with equations in correct notation, research question
Write Hypothesis with null hypothesis if required
Write Materials with specifications and chemical concentrations — Procedure in passive voice at replication level
Present data — significant figures throughout, uncertainty values if recorded
Create graphs — error bars if applicable, best-fit line with equation and R²
BREAK — 8 minutes before analysis
Write Analysis — all calculations with units and sig figs maintained, percent error calculated and interpreted, anomalous data addressed
Write Conclusion — hypothesis evaluation with quantitative evidence, 3 classified error sources, directional effect for each, 2 improvements, 1 follow-up
Significant figures and units audit throughout entire report
Full rubric audit
Format and submit

high_school: Gather all lab records — data table, observations, pre-lab, handout
List required sections — create headings
Write Title, Purpose, and Hypothesis identifying the physical law being tested
Write Materials and Procedure in past-tense numbered steps
Transfer data table with units
Create graphs — labeled axes with units, best-fit line with equation
BREAK — 5 minutes before analysis
Write Analysis — describe trend with numbers, show all calculations with units, explain physical mechanism
Write Conclusion — hypothesis evaluation, 2 error sources, 1 improvement
Rubric check and format
Submit
advanced: Assemble all lab records
Read rubric — note uncertainty requirements, free-body diagram expectations, graph standards
Write Introduction — relevant physical laws and equations stated, research question
Write Hypothesis with quantitative prediction where possible
Write Materials with instrument specifications and Procedure at replication-level detail
Present data — measurements with uncertainty values, correct significant figures
Create graphs — error bars representing measurement uncertainty, best-fit line with equation, R² value, slope interpreted in physical terms
BREAK — 8 minutes
Write Analysis — all calculations with uncertainty propagation, interpret slope and intercept physically, address anomalous data
Write Conclusion — hypothesis evaluation, 3 classified error sources with directional effect, 2 improvements, 1 follow-up question
Verify all units are SI throughout
Full rubric audit
Format and submit

high_school: Get the text and your annotation tools ready — phone away
Preview the reading — read section headings, first sentence of each paragraph, last paragraph
Write one purpose question at the top of your notes before reading
First read — read all the way through, mark only what strongly connects to your purpose question
Second pass — write a margin annotation for each marked passage: what it says and why it matters
Write a 3-sentence summary of the reading in your own words
Check any comprehension questions or annotation requirements from the assignment
Submit or organize for class
advanced: Prepare all texts and open a notes document alongside
Write your analytical lens in your notes before reading — what framework are you applying?
First read — comprehension and initial response, annotate sparingly, write 3-5 summary bullets after
Second read — targeted analysis of marked passages, annotate for technique and effect
Write your reading response if required — analytical claim, evidence with page numbers, analysis, closing question
Annotation quality check — confirm annotations are analytical not just summary
Format and submit

high_school: Get the article and annotation tools ready
Read the title, subheadings, and first and last paragraphs before reading
Write one focus question before reading
Read the article all the way through — circle unfamiliar terms
Look up any terms you circled
Annotate: underline the thesis, mark 2-3 key pieces of evidence
Write 2-3 sentences responding to your focus question
Submit or organize
advanced: Identify the article's genre — academic, journalism, opinion, or policy
Preview structure and establish your analytical lens before reading
First read — track argument structure, annotate main claim and evidence
Second read — analyze rhetorical choices: what does the author do and why?
Write analytical response — specific claim, textual evidence, analysis of technique
Check response quality — every sentence should be analytical not descriptive
Submit

high_school: Clear desk — get pencil, eraser, calculator if allowed, class notes
Survey the whole assignment before starting — count problems, mark familiar vs unfamiliar
Write a time budget at the top — total time divided by number of problems
Do all the familiar problems first — show every step, one operation per line
Quick-check the familiar problems — plug answers back in or use inverse operation
Attempt unfamiliar problems using a relevant worked example from notes — set a 4-minute timer per problem
For any stuck problem: skip, mark it, come back — write a stuck note if still stuck after returning
Final pass — check all answers for correct units, correct format, and reasonableness
Label with name and submit or file in homework folder
advanced: Clear desk — confirm calculator permissions and assemble all reference materials
Survey and triage — label every problem Bracket A (know exactly what to do), B (need to look something up), or C (not sure where to start)
Write time budget — 40% of time to A, 40% to B, 20% to C
Complete all Bracket A problems — write setup line, show every step, box final answer
Work through Bracket B — find a relevant worked example in notes, identify what differs, solve
BREAK — 4-5 minutes before Bracket C
Bracket C — write all given information, write what you need to find, try 2 methods, write a detailed stuck note if neither works
Systematic verification — check answers using a method different from the one used to solve
Label and submit

high_school: Assemble notes, formula sheet if permitted, graphing calculator if allowed
Survey all problems — identify which technique each uses (limit, derivative, integral)
Complete familiar derivative or integral problems — show all steps
For applied problems: draw a diagram first, identify the function, then differentiate or integrate
Check derivatives by differentiating again — check integrals by differentiating your answer
Flag any problem where your answer seems unreasonable in magnitude
Submit with work shown throughout
advanced: Confirm calculator or no-calculator context — this changes which techniques are available
Triage — identify technique required for each problem before starting any
Non-calculator section: work algebraically throughout, leave answers in exact form
Calculator section: show setup and reasoning even if calculator produces the numerical answer
For FRQ-style multi-part problems: treat each part as its own problem with its own answer labeled
Check all answers: derivatives by definition check, definite integrals by FTC, verify bounds on area/accumulation problems
Label and submit with all work shown

high_school: Confirm calculator has statistics functions loaded and is permitted
For each problem: identify the data type first (categorical or quantitative) before choosing a method
Show all calculator setup — function name, values entered, result
Produce any required graphs with labeled axes, title, and scale
For inference problems: identify the procedure by name before calculating
Check that all probabilities are between 0 and 1 and all standard deviations are positive
Write conclusions in context — not just a number, but what it means
Submit with all work and context statements
advanced: Confirm calculator model and functions available
For each problem: state the parameter of interest and identify the appropriate procedure before computing
Show all four steps for every inference problem: State, Plan/Check conditions, Do, Conclude
Check conditions explicitly — do not assume they are met
Write all conclusions in context at the population level with correct statistical language
Distinguish statistical significance from practical significance for any test result
Label and submit

high_school: Get the assignment, your class notes, and a calculator if applicable
For each problem: write the given information and what you are solving for before computing
Write the relevant formula or equation before substituting values
Show all unit conversions — carry units through every calculation step
Check that your answer has the correct units and is a physically reasonable magnitude
For any answer that seems wrong: re-check the formula and unit conversions before re-doing the arithmetic
Submit with work shown
advanced: Identify which scientific law or equation each problem is testing before starting
Write all given information with units — identify what is unknown
Show the symbolic equation before substituting numerical values
Carry significant figures throughout — report final answer to correct sig figs
Include uncertainty if measurement precision is specified
Check answers against expected order of magnitude for the physical quantity
Submit

high_school: Gather all unit notes, returned graded work, and blank practice paper — phone away
Build a complete topic list — check notes, vocabulary lists, learning objectives, and textbook chapter review
Self-test each topic before rating confidence — cover notes and try to explain or solve from memory
Rate each topic 1 (confused), 2 (know when reading), or 3 (can produce without notes)
Active recall on rated-1 topics — write everything from memory, then identify gaps
For any diagram topic: draw it from memory, compare to notes, draw it again
Practice rated-2 topics with application questions — identify the specific step that produced each error
BREAK — 5-7 minutes
Timed mixed practice — 20-25 minutes, no notes, all topic types
Score and categorize all errors by type — vocabulary, concept, application, or careless
Write pre-test reference card — formulas, diagrams, error reminders
Review card once before sleeping
advanced: Assemble all unit materials and released AP exam resources if applicable
Build comprehensive topic inventory — cross-reference with AP CED or official learning objectives
Self-test topics using production standard — rating of 3 means can produce fully from memory without notes
Deep retrieval practice on rated-1 topics — recall from memory, identify gaps, attempt a released FRQ on that topic
Score FRQ against official scoring guidelines — identify specifically which points were missed
Error pattern analysis on rated-2 topics — classify as Formula A, Procedural B, Arithmetic C, or Interpretation D
BREAK — 8-10 minutes before simulation
Full timed simulation at authentic exam conditions and time
Record which topic areas, time periods, and skill types produced the most errors
Build pre-test card from simulation performance data — weakest topics, procedural checklists, strategic reminders
Review card tonight and before the test

high_school: Identify exactly what the quiz covers — ask your teacher or check the assignment
List every term, concept, or skill that could appear
Cover your notes and try to write each definition or solve each type from memory
Mark everything you could not produce — these are your study targets
Review only the marked items — read, cover, reproduce, check
Do 3-5 practice problems or application questions from class notes
Write a half-sheet with the 3-5 most important things to remember before the quiz
advanced: Confirm the exact scope and format of the quiz
Self-test each topic before any re-reading — production standard, not recognition
Focus all study time on rated-1 and rated-2 topics — do not re-study what you already know
For any calculation or procedure: practice it from scratch, show all steps
10-minute timed practice under quiz conditions
Write a brief review card based on what went wrong in the practice

high_school: Gather all unit notes from the entire semester covered — organize by unit
Build a complete topic inventory across all units
Identify which units you are weakest in — allocate most study time there
Self-test topic by topic, unit by unit, from memory
Active recall and diagram practice for rated-1 topics across all units
Application and error-analysis practice for rated-2 topics
BREAK before simulation
Timed mixed practice covering multiple units
Write a comprehensive pre-test card organized by unit
Distribute study across multiple sessions — do not cram in one night
advanced: Build a multi-unit topic inventory cross-referenced with official learning objectives
Rate every topic across all units using production-level standard
Study in unit order — complete one unit before moving to the next
For each unit: recall practice, FRQ attempt, error analysis
Pay special attention to cross-unit connections — midterms often test cumulative reasoning
BREAK — 10 minutes before simulation
Full timed simulation mixing content from all units
Score and analyze errors by unit and skill type
Build a pre-test card organized by unit with your personal error patterns
Distribute preparation across at least 4 separate study sessions

high_school: Map out the full year or semester scope — list every unit covered
Identify which units carry the most weight on the final
Build a topic inventory for each unit
Self-test all topics — identify your weakest areas across the year
Allocate study time by weakness — weakest units get the most time
Active recall and practice for all rated-1 topics
Application practice for rated-2 topics
Build a master review card organized by unit
Timed simulation covering the full year scope
Rest adequately before the exam
advanced: Build a comprehensive year-scope topic inventory aligned to the AP CED or course framework
Identify the highest-weight units and the skill types most frequently tested on released exams
Use released full practice exams as the primary study tool — not your notes
Study in focused unit sprints — one unit per session, complete recall and FRQ practice
Full timed practice exam under authentic conditions
Score using official guidelines — analyze errors by unit, skill type, and question format
Address your specific error patterns with targeted retrieval practice
Build a final pre-exam strategy card with your personal weak areas and reminders
Do not study new content the night before — review your card, sleep, hydrate

high_school: Read all project requirements and confirm the deliverable format — slides, poster, video, or live
Write your research question or thesis before starting any slides
Gather all required sources and take notes organized by your talking points
Build your outline — each section of the presentation as its own row
Create slides or display with one idea per slide — visuals support speech, not replace it
Write speaker notes or talking points for each slide
Practice out loud at least twice — once for content, once for timing
Time yourself — confirm you are within the required window
Prepare for 2-3 likely questions from the audience
Rubric check — confirm all required components are present
Submit written component if required and organize materials for presentation day
advanced: Read all project requirements — clarify deliverable, evaluation criteria, and timing
Develop a specific research question and thesis before any research
Conduct timed research — log all sources as you go
Build a content outline organized around claims, not slides
Design slides or display — one claim per slide, data visualized not listed
Write and practice spoken introduction — practice three times and time it
Prepare responses to the 4-5 most likely challenging questions
Record yourself presenting once and review
Rubric audit — every criterion confirmed
Submit written materials if required
Confirm presentation logistics — time, location, technology setup

high_school: Read the full requirements as a group — confirm the final deliverable and individual responsibilities
Assign specific roles and tasks to each group member in writing
Set internal deadlines at least two days before the actual due date
Complete your individual section without waiting on others
Combine sections and review for consistency of format and argument
Practice the presentation as a complete group at least once
Rubric check as a group — confirm every requirement is met
Submit all required components
advanced: Clarify all requirements as a group on day one — document who does what
Create a shared document with your project structure and everyone's assigned sections
Set an internal deadline 3 days before the actual due date to allow revision
Each member completes their section independently to the internal deadline
Review all sections together — ensure argument consistency and equal contribution
Rehearse as a group — each member practices their portion out loud
Full group rubric audit
Submit all required components and confirm logistics for presentation

high_school: Get the text the discussion is based on and read the prompt carefully
Write your position on the prompt in one or two sentences before doing anything else
Find 2 specific pieces of evidence from the text that support your position
Write one genuine open-ended question you want the class to discuss
Write your post: position, evidence with page number, analysis, closing question
Write at least one reply to a classmate that engages with their argument specifically
Check word count and format requirements
Submit
advanced: Create a prep sheet with four sections: Position, Evidence, Questions, Counterarguments
Write your specific arguable position before reading other posts
Gather 3-4 pieces of evidence with spoken introduction language prepared
Write two questions — one open, one deliberately provocative
Anticipate 2-3 counterpositions and write responses
Write your initial post — argument not summary, specific evidence, closing question
Write a substantive reply that extends or challenges a classmate's specific argument
Check all requirements and submit

high_school: Get the worksheet and your class notes from the relevant unit
Read through the entire worksheet before starting any questions
Answer every question you know immediately — skip and mark the ones you don't
Go back to skipped questions and use your notes to find relevant information
For any question still unanswered: write your best attempt and a note about what confused you
Review all answers for completeness — confirm you answered what was asked
Label with name and submit
advanced: Preview the full worksheet — identify which questions are recall, which are application, and which are analysis
Complete all recall questions first from memory
Work through application questions using class notes and examples
For analysis questions: write your reasoning step by step, not just the answer
Check all answers against the question — confirm you addressed every part
Submit

high_school: Read the prompt carefully — identify genre, required elements, and length
Free write for 8 minutes without editing — follow any idea that interests you
Identify the most specific or interesting moment in your free write
Write a brief outline — beginning, middle, turning point, ending
Write a complete first draft without stopping to edit
BREAK — 3-5 minutes
Read aloud — mark anything that feels generic or that doesn't work
Revise the marked sections — add sensory detail and specificity
Check required elements against the prompt
Final read and submit
advanced: Read the prompt and identify the creative constraint — what is required and what is your freedom?
Free write for 10 minutes — do not self-censor, follow the unexpected
Identify the strongest image, moment, or idea from the free write
Draft 3 possible opening lines — none of them starting with 'I'
Write a structural sketch — what is the movement or arc of this piece?
Write a complete first draft without revising
BREAK — 5 minutes
Read aloud — mark every generic word, passive construction, and stated emotion
Revise for specificity, compression, and voice — show, don't tell
Check that the ending is earned, not just concluded
Final prompt check and submit

high_school: Get the lab handout and open your lab notebook — write title and date
Read only the Background and Purpose sections — write what concept this lab tests
Write your hypothesis in If/Then/Because format before reading the procedure
Identify the Independent Variable, Dependent Variable, and at least 3 Controlled Variables
Read the safety section — write every hazard and required precaution
Read the full procedure — number each step, star any step you have a question about
Write all starred questions in your notebook to ask before the lab
Draw your complete data table with headers (with units) and all rows for every trial
advanced: Open lab notebook — write full heading per course requirements
Write background knowledge from memory before reading the handout
Read Background and Purpose — annotate every scientific term and the research question
Write a mechanistic, falsifiable hypothesis naming specific scientific principles
Operationalize all variables — include measurement instrument, units, and at least 5 controlled variables
Conduct full safety analysis — create a hazard table with PPE and emergency procedures
Read and annotate the procedure — mark timing-critical steps and precision-critical steps
Construct a multi-column data table with trial rows, mean rows, and qualitative observation space

high_school: Read all project requirements and build your milestone calendar today — put every milestone in your phone with reminders
Write at least 3 possible research questions and evaluate each for feasibility
Select the most specific, measurable, and feasible research question
Conduct timed background research — 45 minutes maximum, log every source
Write your hypothesis and complete experimental design — have teacher approve before collecting any data
Execute your experiment following the approved protocol — record data in real time
Take a full day away before beginning analysis
Calculate summary statistics and create all required graphs
Write your report in multiple focused sessions — one major section per session
Rubric check — every required component confirmed
Submit all components
advanced: Read requirements and build a full project management structure with milestone calendar the day it is assigned
Conduct systematic literature review — databases first, journals second, credible journalism third — timed sessions only
Develop and refine research question using four criteria: original, specific, feasible, gap-connected
Write full experimental protocol at replication level — get teacher approval before acquiring materials
Execute experiment following approved protocol exactly — document all deviations
Full day away before analysis — write initial impression of raw data pattern before calculating
Conduct full quantitative analysis including statistical testing with complete work shown
Write report in dedicated sessions across separate days — Discussion section requires the most time
Scientific integrity audit — confirm all claims are evidenced and results are reported honestly
Full rubric audit and submission requirements check
Submit all components and archive materials

high_school: Set up workspace with only Document 1 visible — planning paper ready, phone away
Read the prompt before opening any document — write what it is asking in your own words
Process each document one at a time — write a one-sentence summary and one argument connection for each
Add HAPP notes to each document — author position and how it shaped the document
Look at all document notes together — identify the pattern and write 3 thesis candidates
Assign documents to paragraphs and add one piece of outside historical knowledge per paragraph
BREAK — 4-5 minutes before drafting
Write introduction — historical context, thesis last
Write each body paragraph — topic sentence, cited document with analysis, outside knowledge
Write conclusion — synthesized argument, historical significance
Rubric check — thesis, document use, outside knowledge, HAPP
Format and submit
advanced: Set up planning document with these sections: PROMPT DECONSTRUCTION, DOCUMENT NOTES, CONTEXTUALIZATION, THESIS DRAFTS, OUTSIDE KNOWLEDGE BANK, OUTLINE
Deconstruct the prompt — task verb, time period, reasoning skill, plain-language restatement
Process each document individually — content summary, argument connection, full HAPP, complexity potential
Write 3-5 sentences of contextualization reaching before the document period
Build outside knowledge bank — 6 minutes timed, write everything relevant from memory not in any document
Construct thesis from evidence — historically defensible, establishes a line of reasoning, not just descriptive
Build full outline with AP scoring elements mapped — contextualization, thesis, evidence, HAPP, complexity
BREAK — 6-8 minutes mandatory
Write introduction — contextualization paragraph plus thesis
Write each body paragraph — topic sentence, cited document, analysis, HAPP, outside knowledge
Write complexity paragraph — complicating evidence and how your thesis accounts for it
Write synthesis conclusion
AP rubric audit — verify every scoring point has a specific location in the essay
Format and submit

high_school: Read all project requirements — confirm your role, deliverable, and deadline before anything else
Identify the specific constitutional provision, legal principle, or civic framework that applies to your role
Conduct timed research — 30 minutes maximum, log every source
Build your full position: claim, framework basis, evidence, counterargument, rebuttal
Write your required deliverable — every argument must cite its constitutional or civic basis
BREAK before oral preparation
Write speaking outline and practice your opening out loud at least twice
Prepare responses to 3-4 likely challenges to your position
Rubric check — all components present, arguments grounded in framework
Submit written components — confirm simulation logistics
advanced: Build a project management structure with milestone calendar the day it is assigned
Identify the constitutional provisions, court precedents, and procedural framework with precision
Conduct two-phase research — framework research then issue research, 30-minute timer for each
Develop a sophisticated civic argument with claim, constitutional basis, factual evidence, serious counterargument, and rebuttal
Write the formal deliverable in focused sessions — one major section per session
Civic argument audit — every claim grounded in constitutional or civic framework, counterarguments represented fairly
Prepare extensively for oral component — outline, three practice rounds, record yourself once
Full rubric audit — written and oral components confirmed
Submit all written components
Confirm simulation logistics and review speaking notes before sleeping

high_school: Choose a specific topic — write it as a focused question, not a broad subject
Read two sources about this event — one news report, one additional perspective
Write what the event is and what each source adds — before forming your opinion
Connect this event to something specific from class — name the concept, period, or principle
Write your response: summary paragraph, analysis paragraph, opinion paragraph if required
Check that summary stays factual and analysis goes beyond facts to significance
Add source URLs or titles at the bottom
Submit
advanced: Frame your topic as a specific arguable question
Read three sources — news report, analysis or opinion piece, and a different-perspective source
Note main claim, key evidence, and whose perspective is centered for each source
Identify the tension or debate across your sources — where do they agree and disagree?
Connect to specific course content and form your analytical claim before writing
Write a structured response — factual foundation, perspective analysis, course connection, significance conclusion
Unsupported claims audit — every position must be evidenced
Add citations and submit
